Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

derivations.claim: For each real component polynomial $p$ of degree at most $M-1$, $p$ and $I_Mp$ have the same $M$ nodal data and degree bound, so uniqueness in [F2] gives $I_Mp=p$; all reproduction uses below are componentwise. The stage equations in [F1] and boundedness of $f$ on the tube first give $U_i-u=O(h)$. The exact path satisfies $y'=f(t,y)$ by [F5]. We prove by induction on $s=1,\ldots,M$ that there are vector polynomials $P_s$ of degree at most $s$ such that $U_i=u+\sum_{r=1}^s h^rP_r(c_i)+O(h^{s+1})$ uniformly over the finite node set. For the induction step, substitute the expansion through order $s$ into each scalar coordinate of $f(t+hc_j,U_j)$ and apply the scalar Taylor supplier [F3] at $(t,u)$. Each coefficient of $h^m$ is a polynomial in $c_j$ of degree at most $m$, because every time increment contributes one factor $c_jh$ and each state coefficient at order $r$ has degree at most $r$. For $m\le M-1$, [F2] makes interpolation exact on that coefficient; the row identity $Q_{ij}=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j$ then integrates it to a polynomial in $c_i$ of degree at most $m+1$. Multiplication by the outer $h$ gives the next $P_{m+1}$. Taylor remainders are uniform on the fixed compact tube, and the stated local branch supplies the stage solution.

The coefficient construction in step 1.1 and its Taylor expansion give vector polynomials $R_m$ of degree at most $m$ with $f(t+hc_j,U_j)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}h^mR_m(c_j)+\delta_j(h)$, where $\max_j\|\delta_j(h)\|=O(h^M)$. Apply componentwise reproduction from [F2] and define $e_h(\tau)=\sum_j\ell_j(\tau)\delta_j(h)$. Then $I_Mg_h(\tau)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}h^mR_m(\tau)+e_h(\tau)$ and every derivative of $e_h$ through order $M-1$ is $O(h^M)$, because its basis is fixed. Substituting into the defining integral in [F1], rather than identifying a degree-$M$ polynomial from only its $M$ stage values, gives $u_h(\tau)=u+\sum_{s=1}^M h^sP_s(\tau)+R_h(\tau)$ with $P_s(\tau)=\int_0^\tau R_{s-1}(a)\,da$ and $R_h(\tau)=h\int_0^\tau e_h(a)\,da$. These are the same integrated coefficients used in step 1.1 through the row integrals $Q_{ij}$. Thus $\deg P_s\le s$, $P_s(0)=0$, $\|R_h\|_\infty=O(h^{M+1})$, and for $1\le j\le M$, $R_h^{(j)}=h e_h^{(j-1)}=O(h^{M+1})$. Differentiating the expansion annihilates every term with $s<j$ and bounds the remaining terms by $O(h^j)$. Hence $\|u_h^{(j)}\|_\infty=O(h^j)$ for $1\le j\le M$; derivatives above $M$ vanish by the defining integrated cardinal sum. This argument also covers $M=1$ and a node at zero.

Repeated chain and product rules from [F3] express each coordinate of $g_h^{(j)}$ as a finite sum of derivatives of that coordinate of $f$ applied to derivatives of $(t+h\tau,u_h(\tau))$ whose orders add to $j$. Each argument derivative of order $s\le M$ is $O(h^s)$ by step 2.1; higher derivatives vanish for the polynomial state and affine time coordinate. The bounded derivatives in [F4] therefore give $\|g_h^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_jh^j$ through $j=2M$.

For $j<M$, subtract from each coordinate of $g_h$ its Taylor polynomial of degree $M-1$ at $0$. Its remainder and its first $j$ derivatives are $O(h^M)$ by step 3.1 and the one-variable Taylor remainder in [F3]. Interpolation reproduces that Taylor polynomial by [F2]; derivatives of the interpolated remainder are bounded by the fixed constants $\max_{\tau}\sum_i|\ell_i^{(j)}(\tau)|$, so $(I_Mg_h-g_h)^{(j)}=O(h^M)$ coordinatewise. Multiplying by $h$ gives $r_h^{(j)}=O(h^{M+1})\le O(h^{j+1})$ for $j<M$ and $h\le1$. For $M\le j\le2M$, $I_Mg_h$ has degree at most $M-1$, so its $j$th derivative vanishes and $r_h^{(j)}=-h g_h^{(j)}=O(h^{j+1})$ by step 3.1.

For the distinct nodes and cardinal polynomials in [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]], every entry of $Q$, every component of $b$, and the Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_M$ is a finite real number.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.

   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

about one $x$ at a time.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$

$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$

The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$

$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$

$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$

$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Fix $M$ distinct nodes in $[0,1]$, a time $t$, and an exact IVP solution $y$ on an interval $[t,t+h_0]$ for some $h_0>0$, with initial state $u=y(t)$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be defined on a neighborhood of a compact tube containing this exact trajectory and the collocation stages. Assume each scalar coordinate of $f$ has continuous partial derivatives through total order $2M+1$, all bounded on the tube. Smoothness of vector-valued functions and their derivative bounds here and below are componentwise; the scalar Taylor supplier is applied to each coordinate, and finite-dimensional coordinate bounds give the stated Euclidean norm bounds. Assume the collocation stage branch exists and is locally unique in this tube for all sufficiently small $h\le h_0$. Let $u_h$ be the collocation polynomial from [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]], and set
$$g_h(\tau)=f(t+h\tau,u_h(\tau)),\qquad r_h(\tau)=u_h'(\tau)-h g_h(\tau).$$
For $1\le j\le M$, $\|u_h^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_jh^j$; for $j>M$, $u_h^{(j)}=0$. For $0\le j\le2M$, $\|g_h^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_jh^j$ (with $h^0=1$), and
$$\|r_h^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_j h^{j+1}.$$
The constants depend on the fixed node set and its cardinal-basis derivative bounds; no uniformity in $M$ is asserted.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], let $Q_m$ be its Gaussian rule, and let
$f\in C^{2m}([a,b],\mathbb R)$. Then there is $\xi\in(a,b)$ such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}f(x)\,d\mu(x)-Q_m(f) =\frac{f^{(2m)}(\xi)}{(2m)!_{\mathbb R}} \int_{[a,b]}p_m(x)^2\,d\mu(x), $$
where $p_m(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(X-x_i)$ is the monic node polynomial and
$(2m)!_{\mathbb R}:=\prod_{j=1}^{2m}j$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $f_k:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous for
every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ has its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t)=|s-t|$. If $f_k\to f$ uniformly on $X$, then
$f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].
Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $M\ge1$, Lebesgue measure on the relative Borel space $[0,1]$ is Gaussian quadrature moment data of order $2M$ in the sense of [[def-gauss-moment-data]].
Assume Countable Choice. Let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its Riemann integral and its Lebesgue integral with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ both exist and are equal.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

derivations.claim: Let $y_h(s)=y(t+hs)$ and $e(s)=y_h(s)-u_h(s)$. Define the averaged Jacobian $A(s)=\int_0^1D_yf(t+hs,u_h(s)+\theta e(s))\,d\theta$ and $B(s)=hA(s)$. For each unit vector $v\in\mathbb R^d$, the vector integral inequality [F8] gives $\|A(s)v\|_2\le\int_0^1\|D_yf(t+hs,u_h(s)+\theta e(s))v\|_2\,d\theta\le L$. Taking the supremum over unit $v$ proves $\|A(s)\|_{op}\le L$ and hence $\|B(s)\|_{op}\le hL$. Applying the scalar FTC to each coordinate along the segment gives $f(t+hs,y_h(s))-f(t+hs,u_h(s))=A(s)e(s)$. With $r_h=u_h'-hg_h$, [F13] and [F1] give $e'=Be-r_h$, $e(0)=0$.

For a continuous matrix function $X$ set $\|X\|_\infty:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|X(s)\|_{op}$. Define $(TX)(s)=\int_s^1X(\tau)B(\tau)\,d\tau$ entrywise. For any unit vector $v$, the vector integral inequality [F8] and submultiplicativity in [A1] give
$$\|(TX-TY)(s)v\|_2\le\int_s^1\|(X-Y)(\tau)B(\tau)v\|_2\,d\tau\le hL\|X-Y\|_\infty.$$
Taking the supremum over unit $v$ and $s$ proves $\|TX-TY\|_\infty\le hL\|X-Y\|_\infty$. For $hL\le1/2$, $T$ is a contraction. Starting with $P_0=I$, set $P_{n+1}=I+TP_n$. Successive differences are bounded by $2^{-n}\|TP_0\|_\infty$, so their entries are uniformly Cauchy; [F9] gives an entrywise limit and the geometric tail bound makes convergence uniform. Each iterate is continuous and [F7] makes the limit $P$ continuous. Passing to the limit in $P_{n+1}=I+TP_n$ gives $P=I+TP$, hence $P'=-PB$ and $P(1)=I$ by applying [F6] to each matrix entry. If $P$ and $\widetilde P$ both solve it, $D=P-\widetilde P=TD$ implies $\|D\|_\infty\le\frac12\|D\|_\infty$, so $D=0$; also $P=I+TP$ gives $\|P\|_\infty\le2$.

The normalized exact path satisfies $y_h'=h f(t+hs,y_h(s))=O(h)$ by [F13] and [A1]. If $y_h^{(r)}=O(h^r)$ for $1\le r\le j$, the chain rule [F5] writes the $j$th derivative of $f(t+hs,y_h(s))$ as a finite sum whose argument-derivative orders total $j$; each term is $O(h^j)$. Differentiating the IVP identity gives $y_h^{(j+1)}=O(h^{j+1})$. Induction proves $y_h^{(j)}=O(h^j)$ through order $2M$.

The path $u_h+\theta(y_h-u_h)$ between the collocation polynomial and exact path has normalized derivatives of order $j\le M-1$ of size $O(h^j)$ by [F2] and step 2.2. Repeated chain and product rules for $D_yf$, then integration over $0\le\theta\le1$ with uniform remainders on the compact tube, give $\|A^{(j)}\|_\infty=O(h^j)$ and $\|B^{(j)}\|_\infty=O(h^{j+1})$ for $0\le j<M$.

Differentiating $P'=-PB$ entrywise gives $P^{(j)}=-\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}\binom{j-1}{k}P^{(k)}B^{(j-1-k)}$ for $1\le j\le M$. Induction from $\|P\|_\infty\le2$ and step 3.1 yields $\|P^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_jh^j$. Apply the scalar Taylor formula [F4] to every matrix entry to get a matrix polynomial $q$ of degree at most $M-1$ with $\|P-q\|_\infty\le Ch^M$ and $\|q^{(j)}\|_\infty\le C_jh^j$ for $j<M$. Finite dimensionality combines the entrywise bounds in the induced operator norm.

By [F1], $b_j=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds$; by [F11] the Gauss weights are $w_j=\int\ell_j\,d\lambda$. The continuous-integral agreement [F12] gives $b_j=w_j$. Uniqueness of the monic orthogonal polynomial [F14] makes the order-$2M$ and order-$(2M-1)$ branch nodes identical, so [F3] applies to this tableau. By [F2], $\|g_h-I_Mg_h\|_\infty=O(h^M)$. The cardinal interpolation [F10] gives degree at most $2M-2$ for each coordinate of $qI_Mg_h$, and [F3] therefore gives, coordinatewise, $\int qI_Mg_h=\sum_jb_jq(c_j)g_h(c_j)$. Split the weighted defect integral entrywise as $\int_0^1P(g_h-I_Mg_h)=\int_0^1(P-q)(g_h-I_Mg_h)+\left(\int_0^1qg_h-\int_0^1qI_Mg_h\right)$.

The first integral in step 5.1 is $O(h^{2M})$ by step 4.1 and $\|g_h-I_Mg_h\|_\infty=O(h^M)$. For each scalar coordinate, the parenthesized term is the Gauss quadrature error for that coordinate of $qg_h$. Leibniz' rule [F5] and the bounds $q^{(j)}=O(h^j)$ and $g_h^{(j)}=O(h^j)$ show $(qg_h)^{(2M)}=O(h^{2M})$ coordinatewise, so the scalar remainder [F3] bounds every coordinate error by $O(h^{2M})$. Since there are finitely many coordinates, the vector integral is $O(h^{2M})$ in Euclidean norm. Hence $\int_0^1P(g_h-I_Mg_h)=O(h^{2M})$.

By step 1.1, $e'=Be-r_h$, and step 2.1 gives $P'=-PB$, $P(1)=I$. Apply the product rule entrywise to obtain $(Pe)'=-Pr_h$; the scalar FTC on each coordinate and $e(0)=0$ give $e(1)=-\int_0^1Pr_h=h\int_0^1P(g_h-I_Mg_h)$. Step 6.1 bounds this by $O(h^{2M+1})$, and [F1] identifies $u_h(1)$ as the collocation endpoint. This proves the local defect bound.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interval-measure formula. For Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, the one-node Gaussian quadrature rule has node $c_1=1/2$ and weight $b_1=1$. Its one-stage collocation tableau therefore has $Q_{11}=1/2$ and endpoint weight $b_1=1$.

Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $f$ be $L$-Lipschitz in state on a common invariant stage tube, and let the collocation stage branches for initial states $u,v$ lie in that tube. If $hL\|Q\|_\infty\le1/2$, then
$$\|U(u)-U(v)\|_{\infty,2}\le2\|u-v\|_2.$$
Consequently the collocation step map $\Psi_h(u)=u+h\sum_jb_j f(t+c_jh,U_j(u))$ satisfies
$$\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+2hL\|b\|_1)\|u-v\|_2,\qquad \|b\|_1:=\sum_j|b_j|.$$

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. $$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

$$Z\longmapsto \mathbf1u+hQ_\Delta F(Z)+h(Q-Q_\Delta)F(V)$$
maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, and assume the stage field $F(U)=(f(t+c_i h,U_i))_{i=1}^M$ is $L$-Lipschitz there for some $L\ge0$. Put
$$a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty,\qquad q=\frac{hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty}{1-a}.$$

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].
Assume Countable Choice. Let $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its Riemann integral and its Lebesgue integral with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ both exist and are equal.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue interval-measure formula. Fix $M\ge1$, the $M$-node Gauss rule for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$, a time $t$, and an exact IVP solution $y$ on an interval containing $[t,t+h_0]$ for some $h_0>0$, with initial state $u=y(t)$. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be an IVP vector field on a neighborhood of a common compact convex tube, let $u_h$ be its Gauss collocation polynomial for this exact start, and put $g_h(s)=f(t+hs,u_h(s))$. Assume each scalar coordinate of $f$ has continuous partial derivatives through total order $2M+1$, all bounded on the tube; vector smoothness and derivatives below are understood componentwise, with scalar Taylor and quadrature results applied coordinatewise. The tube contains the exact path, $u_h$, and every segment joining them, and the collocation branch and tube are uniform for sufficiently small $h\le h_0$. Use the induced Euclidean operator norm $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$, and assume $\|D_yf\|_{op}\le L$ on the tube. Then its endpoint defect satisfies
$$\|y(t+h)-u_h(1)\|_2\le C h^{2M+1},$$
where $C$ may depend on the fixed nodes and on $M$.

Let $M,d\ge1$, let $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$ be distinct collocation nodes, and let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_M$ be their cardinal polynomials from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
$$Q_{ij}:=\int_0^{c_i}\ell_j(s)\,ds,\qquad b_j:=\int_0^1\ell_j(s)\,ds.$$
The matrix $Q\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ and vector $b\in\mathbb R^M$ are the collocation tableau coefficients. For an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$ on the open domain of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], write
$$F_j(U):=f(t+c_jh,U_j),\qquad QF(U):=\left(\sum_{j=1}^M Q_{ij}F_j(U)\right)_{i=1}^M.$$
All displayed integrals use the oriented Riemann convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. In particular $Q_{ij}=0$ when $c_i=0$, and the integral in $u_h$ vanishes at $\tau=0$. The collocation stages and endpoint are the implicit Runge–Kutta equations of [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] with $A=Q$, nodes $c$, and weights $b$:
$$U=\mathbf1u+hQF(U),\qquad \Psi_h(t,u)=u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U).$$
The associated collocation polynomial on normalized time $\tau\in[0,1]$ is
$$u_h(\tau):=u+h\int_0^\tau\sum_{j=1}^M\ell_j(s)F_j(U)\,ds.$$
Thus $u_h(c_i)=U_i$, $u_h'(c_i)=hF_i(U)$, and $u_h(1)=\Psi_h(t,u)$ whenever $U$ is an admissible solution. This definition alone asserts no branch existence or uniqueness.

For interpolation estimates define the **Lebesgue constant** of this fixed node set by
$$\Lambda_M:=\max_{0\le s\le1}\sum_{j=1}^M|\ell_j(s)|.$$
For a real matrix $A$, write $\|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$. These constants depend on the nodes and on $M$; no uniform-in-$M$ bound is part of the definition.
For the distinct nodes and cardinal polynomials in [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]], every entry of $Q$, every component of $b$, and the Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_M$ is a finite real number.
Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $M\ge1$, Lebesgue measure on the relative Borel space $[0,1]$ is Gaussian quadrature moment data of order $2M$ in the sense of [[def-gauss-moment-data]].

derivations.claim: By [F5] under [A1] the chosen Gaussian rule has admissible Lebesgue moment data. Fact [F1] gives its nodes and cardinal-integral weights, and [F4] makes the matching collocation tableau finite and defined.

The smoothness, common-tube, and branch hypotheses of [F3] are precisely those in the Statement and [A2]. The lemma therefore gives $\|y(t+h)-\Psi_h(y(t))\|_2\le Ch^{2M+1}$, which is the claimed exact-start local defect estimate. Agreement of the integral conventions is [F2].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be the open time-state domain of an IVP $y'=f(t,y)$, with $d\ge1$. The inputs are a time $t\in\mathbb R$, an initial state $u\in\mathbb R^d$ with $(t,u)\in D$, a step $h>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, distinct ordered nodes $0\le c_1<\cdots<c_M\le1$, a predictor (default $U^0=\mathbf1u$), a Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, a tolerance $\mathrm{tol}>0$, an integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and a supplied stage set $\mathcal C$. A stage vector $U$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,U_j)\in D$ for every $j$.

After validating the node data, form the collocation tableau $Q,b$ of [[def-collocation-quadrature-tableau]]. Let $c_0=0$, $\Delta c_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$, and define the left-Euler node-subinterval preconditioner by its initial column $a_i=c_1$ and stage block
$$ (Q_\Delta)_{ij}=\begin{cases}\Delta c_{j+1},&j<i,\\0,&j\ge i.\end{cases} $$
The stage block is strictly lower triangular. In augmented notation, set $\widehat Q=(0\mid Q)$, $\widehat Q_\Delta=(a\mid Q_\Delta)$, and $\widehat F(U)=(f(t,u),F(U))$. One sweep is
$$U^{k+1}=\mathbf1u+h\widehat Q_\Delta\widehat F(U^{k+1})+h(\widehat Q-\widehat Q_\Delta)\widehat F(U^k).$$
The fixed initial-column contributions cancel, so the procedure below does not evaluate $F_0=f(t,u)$. For a stage vector $U$, write $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$. Since $Q_\Delta$ is strictly lower triangular, for fixed previous stages $U^k$ the unique new stages are computed in increasing $i$ by the forward recursion
$$U_i^{k+1}=u+h\sum_{j<i}(Q_\Delta)_{ij}F_j(U^{k+1})+h\sum_{j=1}^M(Q_{ij}-(Q_\Delta)_{ij})F_j(U^k),\quad i=1,\ldots,M.$$

Use $\|V\|_{\infty,2}=\max_i\|V_i\|_2$ and $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. The supplied set $\mathcal C$ must be a nonempty closed product ball of admissible stage vectors, contain the predictor, be invariant under each inner stage map and outer sweep, and have an $L$-Lipschitz stage field $F(U)=(F_j(U))_{j=1}^M$ in this norm. After forming $Q_\Delta$, compute $a=hL\|Q_\Delta\|_\infty$. If $a\ge1$, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. For $a<1$, compute $q=hL\|Q-Q_\Delta\|_\infty/(1-a)$; if $q\ge1$ or invariance is not certified, return `contraction-not-certified` with no accepted endpoint. The exact procedure is:

1. Reject repeated, unordered, or out-of-range nodes as `invalid-node-data` before forming the tableau.
2. Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ from the valid nodes and apply the contraction and invariance checks described above.
3. If the predictor is outside $\mathcal C$ or any required stage evaluation $(t+c_jh,U_j)$ lies outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint.
4. Evaluate and store all $M$ values $F_j(U^0)$ once.
5. If $K=0$, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; no residual test has been performed.
6. For $k=0,1,\ldots,K-1$, compute $U^{k+1}$ in increasing stage order using the displayed recursion, reusing the stored $F(U^k)$ and evaluating each new $F_j(U^{k+1})$ once. If a new stage is outside $D$, return `inadmissible-stage` and no accepted endpoint. Then compute $r_k=\|U^{k+1}-U^k\|_{\infty,2}$. If $r_k\le(1-q)\,\mathrm{tol}$, return status `residual-tolerance-met`, the stage vector $U^k$, and endpoint $u+h\sum_{j=1}^M b_jF_j(U^k)$. If this is the $K$th sweep and the test failed, return `iteration-budget-exhausted` and no accepted endpoint; otherwise use $U^{k+1}$ and its stored field values as the next iterate.

These statuses report only the stated branch outcome; they do not assert convergence when a check fails.

Form $Q,b,Q_\Delta$ once per invocation and retain their coefficients through the sweep loop. Retain the old and current stage vectors and their field values while computing a sweep and testing its residual. On continuation, reuse these buffers for the next sweep; on acceptance, use the retained $U^k$ and $F(U^k)$ for the returned stage vector and endpoint in step 6. Perform the displayed operations in exact real arithmetic.

Consider the procedure of [[alg-explicit-left-euler-sdc-sweep]] with $M,d\ge1$ and budget $K\ge0$. Count one **stage call** for each instructed evaluation of $F_j(U)=f(t+c_jh,U_j)$, even when different calls happen to have equal arguments. Generating the supplied predictor and constructing or checking external admissibility, set-membership or invariance certificates are outside this call count. Assume each invoked evaluation and check returns. The following counts apply to any supplied predictor, including the default constant predictor.

- An exit at the node, contraction, invariance or predictor-admissibility checks before step 4 uses zero instructed stage calls. A run completing step 4 uses $M$ predictor calls. If $K=0$, it then returns `iteration-budget-exhausted`, with no residual test and no accepted endpoint.
- If predictor evaluation and exactly $s$ full sweeps complete, with no incomplete sweep, the run uses exactly $M(s+1)$ stage calls, where $0\le s\le K$. If the next sweep instead exits at an inadmissible stage after evaluating a prefix of $p$ new stages, where $0\le p<M$ and $s<K$, the count is exactly $M(s+1)+p$.
- Hence every execution uses at most $M(K+1)$ instructed stage calls. Equality holds for a run completing predictor evaluation and all $K$ sweeps, including the $K=0$ case after predictor evaluation. Acceptance after $s\ge1$ completed sweeps returns $U^{s-1}$; forming its endpoint uses the cached $F(U^{s-1})$ and adds no stage call. No $F_0=f(t,u)$ call is required.

For direct dense evaluation of the prescribed finite sums, the stored tableau and preconditioner use $O(M^2)$ real coefficients, and old/current stage and derivative buffers use $O(Md)$ real scalars. A complete sweep uses $O(M^2d)$ scalar arithmetic in addition to its $M$ stage calls. Its residual requires $O(Md)$ scalar arithmetic, at most $M$ square roots and $O(M)$ comparisons; the accepted endpoint requires $O(Md)$ further arithmetic and no stage calls. These bounds also bound any evaluated prefix of a failed sweep. After the quadrature data are supplied, forming the preconditioner, coefficient differences and contraction row norms uses $O(M^2)$ scalar arithmetic and absolute-value operations. Including default constant-predictor initialization, all direct algebraic work through any exit is bounded by $O(M^2+(K+1)M^2d)$, with at most $KM$ square roots for residuals; scalar absolute values and loop/comparison work obey the same asymptotic bound. The storage bound is independent of $K$ when buffers are reused as instructed.

These bounds exclude the work and internal storage of evaluating $f$, constructing the polynomial quadrature data, generating a supplied nondefault predictor, and performing the external domain/set/certificate checks. They do not bound those unspecified tasks or assert that a failed execution completed $K$ sweeps. All counts concern exact real arithmetic and give no floating-point roundoff guarantee.

If the run stops after $s>0$ completed sweeps with no incomplete sweep, each adds exactly $M$ evaluations because its $M$ new stage states are evaluated once and the previous $F(U^j)$ values are reused. Thus the total is $M+sM=M(s+1)$, and for $s\le K$ this is at most $M(K+1)$, attained if all $K$ sweeps complete. A failed run with a partially evaluated sweep is counted by its actual prefix as in [F2], and still obeys that bound. Acceptance after $s\ge1$ sweeps returns $U^{s-1}$ and uses its cached endpoint derivatives with no additional calls.

The stored dense matrices $Q,Q_\Delta$ each have $M^2$ real entries, so their storage is $O(M^2)$; retaining old/current stage vectors and their derivative values takes $O(Md)$ additional scalar storage. Each forward-recursion stage has two sums with at most $2M$ vector terms in total, for at most $O(M^2d)$ scalar arithmetic per sweep. Residual formation adds $O(Md)$ scalar arithmetic and at most $M$ square roots; an accepted endpoint adds $O(Md)$ arithmetic and no new field evaluations. These are the proved counts in [F2]. They omit the cost of evaluating $f$, constructing the polynomial quadrature data (which depends on their representation), supplied predictor generation, and external admissibility/invariance certification and their internal storage. The model uses exact real arithmetic and gives no floating-point roundoff guarantee.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and
